questions.q: Why are staging table columns typically loosely typed (often wide strings), even when the final warehouse column is a strict INT or DATE?
options: So the load doesn't fail just because a source value arrived in an unexpected format — problems get fixed later in Transform
Because SQL Server cannot store integers in staging schemas
Because loosely typed columns automatically enforce data quality
Because it makes the staging table smaller on disk
questions.explain: Staging's job is to safely land whatever the source sends. Strict typing at the staging stage would make the extract itself fail on messy source data instead of catching it downstream.

questions.q: What does a typical staging table deliberately omit compared to a warehouse table?
options: Primary keys, foreign keys, and check constraints
Any column names at all
The ability to be queried by SQL
A LoadDate audit column
questions.explain: Staging tables skip most constraints — foreign key lookups to dimensions and other validation happen in later transformation steps, not at staging load time.

options: Emptying a staging table with TRUNCATE, then bulk-inserting the newly extracted rows on every run
Permanently deleting the warehouse's fact tables after each report
Renaming a staging table to a new name on every load
Adding a new column to a staging table on every run
questions.explain: Truncate-and-reload clears out the previous load's rows before loading the current batch, which is fast and guarantees rows from two different load runs never mix.

questions.q: When is truncate-and-reload the WRONG choice for a staging table?
options: When that staging table itself needs to preserve a previous load's rows to diff against, such as feeding a Type 2 SCD compare step
Whenever the staging table has more than 10 columns
It's never wrong — truncate-and-reload should always be used
Whenever the source system is a flat file instead of a database
questions.explain: A staging table that needs to compare the current extract to the prior load's data (common ahead of an SCD Type 2 change-detection step) can't be truncated before that comparison happens.

questions.q: Why should a staging table's column names closely mirror the source system's column names?
options: So anyone reading the staging table can tell at a glance which source column each one came from, before any transformation renames anything
Because SQL Server requires staging and source columns to have identical names
Because mirrored names make the columns automatically typed correctly
Renaming columns in staging is not technically possible
questions.explain: Keeping staging column names aligned with the source makes the ETL process traceable — you can see exactly where each staged value came from before any transformation logic touches it.
